title: Environment, Condemned Material, Waste and By-products

lessons.title: Condemned material and by-products
lessons.html:
Not everything becomes meat

When an animal is slaughtered, only part of it becomes meat. The rest is by-products (useful materials) or waste. Some parts, or even whole carcasses, are condemned by the meat inspector because they are not safe to eat.

Condemned material

The meat inspector condemns meat or organs that are diseased, damaged, contaminated or otherwise unfit, such as livers with parasites, bruised meat, abscesses, or a carcass from a sick animal.

  • Condemned material is put into special marked containers, often red or clearly labelled.
  • It is kept apart from edible meat and must never go back into the food chain.
  • It is often stained or denatured so that no one can use it as food.
  • It goes to an approved disposal method, such as rendering, incineration or an approved disposal site, as the abattoir's procedure says.
  • Only the meat inspector decides what is condemned. Never take condemned material home or sell it.

By-products

By-productUse
HidesLeather; salted and sold to tanneries
Edible offal (liver, heart, tongue, tripe)Sold as food after inspection
BloodBlood meal for animal feed or fertiliser
Bones, fat and inedible partsRendered into meat-and-bone meal and tallow
Horns and hoovesVarious products
Rumen contents and manureCompost

By-products earn money for the abattoir. Handle them cleanly and put each one in its correct container so their value is not lost.

Keep by-products and condemned material apart from each other too. If condemned material is mixed with hides or edible offal, the whole container may have to be condemned and the abattoir loses money. When you are not sure which container to use, ask your supervisor.

lessons.title: Waste and protecting the environment
lessons.html:
Abattoir waste

An abattoir produces a lot of waste every day: blood, wastewater, rumen contents, manure from the lairage, fat, hair, and packaging. If waste is not managed, it causes serious problems.

Why waste is a danger

  • Water pollution: blood and wastewater are very rich in organic material. If they reach a river or dam they use up the oxygen, kill fish and spread disease. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 protects water resources.
  • Flies and rats: they breed in waste and carry germs back onto meat.
  • Bad smells, which upset neighbours.
  • Disease: waste from sick animals can spread disease to people and animals.

Good waste practice on the slaughter floor

  1. Collect blood in the blood trough or tank; do not let it run into the drains.
  2. Dry-clean first: scrape and shovel solid waste (fat, meat scraps, rumen contents) into bins before hosing. This saves water and keeps solids out of the drains.
  3. Keep drains open and the screens in place, so solids are caught.
  4. Put each type of waste in its marked container: condemned, inedible, edible by-product, general waste.
  5. Close bins and remove them from the slaughter area regularly.
  6. Do not mix chemical waste with organic waste.

Saving water and energy

  • Close taps and hoses when not in use; report leaks.
  • Use the right nozzle so you clean well with less water.
  • Close chiller doors quickly to save electricity.

Your responsibility

If you see blood or waste running to a river, a full or broken bin, or a blocked drain, tell your supervisor straight away.

Key points

  • Only the meat inspector condemns meat; condemned material never returns to the food chain.
  • By-products like hides, blood and bones have value: keep them clean and sorted.
  • Blood and wastewater pollute rivers if not controlled.
  • Dry-clean solids before hosing and keep drain screens in place.
  • Report leaks, spills and full bins.
